# Education in Poland – Concise Summary
Poland’s education system is structured around compulsory schooling, which typically begins at age six or seven and continues through primary school (szkoła podstawowa) for eight years, following reforms implemented in 2017 that abolished the former three-year junior high/middle school (gimnazjum) system. After primary education, students enter upper secondary education, which includes general secondary schools (liceum, four years), technical schools (technikum, five years), and basic vocational schools (zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa, three years). Graduates of liceum and technikum attain the "Matura," granting access to higher education; vocational routes allow for further study to attain the Matura.
Tertiary education in Poland largely follows the Bologna process, offering a three-year bachelor’s degree and a two-year master’s degree, with certain fields using long-cycle programs. Doctoral degrees generally require three years of study, and teacher training typically takes three years at a teacher training college. University grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (failing) to 5.0 (highest), with grading conducted every semester. Foreign language education is emphasized, with students typically learning one or two foreign languages, and there are schools for national minorities. Historical context highlights Poland’s early commitment to education, with institutions like Jagiellonian University (est. 1364) and reforms dating back to the 18th century.
